author: Antibiotogram editors
status: Teaching commentary — not a dosing or treatment recommendation

AMP.summary: Classic cell-wall drug for susceptible Enterococcus faecalis and selected streptococci.
AMP.shines: Best remembered for enterococcal infections, especially when paired for endocarditis synergy.
AMP.trap: Do not expect cephalosporin-like Gram-negative coverage. It is narrow and easy to over-credit.

TZP.summary: Strong single-agent breadth for many hospital infections, especially when anaerobes matter.
TZP.shines: Useful when you need Pseudomonas plus anaerobic coverage in one bag.
TZP.trap: Do not lean on it for serious ESBL infections just because the lab says susceptible.

SAM.summary: Good for oral flora and anaerobes, and worth remembering because sulbactam itself matters for Acinetobacter.
SAM.shines: Helpful teaching drug for aspiration syndromes, bite wounds, and CRAB discussions.
SAM.trap: The useful CRAB idea is the sulbactam exposure, not magical broad coverage against everything.

CFZ.summary: One of the cleanest answers for MSSA bacteremia and skin-soft tissue infections.
CFZ.shines: A good reminder that a narrow beta-lactam often beats a broader agent for MSSA.
CFZ.trap: Do not mentally upgrade it into MRSA or Enterococcus coverage.

CRO.summary: Strong daily cephalosporin for many community infections and a frequent hospital default.
CRO.shines: Great teaching drug for pneumococcus, H. influenzae, meningitis patterns, and mixed community syndromes.
CRO.trap: It does not cover Pseudomonas and it is weak for AmpC derepression problems like Enterobacter cloacae complex.

FEP.summary: Broad cephalosporin with anti-pseudomonal activity and a better teaching role around inducible AmpC.
FEP.shines: Useful when the trainee needs to separate cefepime from ceftriaxone in Enterobacter-type organisms.
FEP.trap: It still does not cover anaerobes and it is not a universal answer for all resistant Gram-negatives.

CPT.summary: A cephalosporin that matters because it reaches MRSA and often appears in salvage combinations.
CPT.shines: High-yield for MRSA teaching and for the daptomycin-plus-ceftaroline synergy concept.
CPT.trap: Do not confuse anti-MRSA activity with anti-pseudomonal activity. It does not solve that problem.

CT.summary: A modern choice that trainees should associate with difficult Pseudomonas rather than routine use.
CT.shines: Good mental anchor for MDR Pseudomonas when standard anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams start failing.
CT.trap: It is not the same as ceftaroline and it is not an anaerobe solution.

MEM.summary: Core reference carbapenem for ESBL and many severe Gram-negative infections.
MEM.shines: Useful benchmark when trainees need to compare newer BL/BLI agents against an old standard.
MEM.trap: Do not assume all carbapenem-resistant organisms are still partly carbapenem treatable.

CA.summary: High-yield reserve agent for KPC and some OXA-48-like CRE discussions.
CA.shines: A key teaching drug for serine carbapenemases and why mechanism matters.
CA.trap: It does not fix metallo-beta-lactamases like NDM.

AA.summary: The standout option on this page for MBL logic, especially NDM-heavy salvage scenarios.
AA.shines: Excellent concept drug for explaining why aztreonam plus inhibitor logic matters in MBL infections.
AA.trap: It is still a specialist-space drug and should not be mentally promoted into a routine broad-spectrum default.

FDC.summary: Siderophore cephalosporin that belongs in the conversation when resistant Gram-negatives have exhausted standard options.
FDC.shines: Good for NDM, XDR Pseudomonas, and CRAB discussions where trainees need a modern salvage anchor.
FDC.trap: Coverage on paper does not remove the need for source control, repeat susceptibility checks, and specialist input.

VAN.summary: The usual baseline comparator for MRSA and severe Gram-positive infections.
VAN.shines: Useful as the starting point for thinking through MRSA, enterococcal coverage, and C. difficile PO-specific use.
VAN.trap: Remember that IV vancomycin and oral vancomycin solve very different problems.

DAP.summary: Important for MRSA salvage and VRE, especially outside the lung.
DAP.shines: High-yield when paired with ceftaroline in persistent MRSA bacteremia or VISA-type problems.
DAP.trap: Do not reach for it in pneumonia. The lung is the classic catch.

LZD.summary: A powerful oral-capable Gram-positive drug that trainees remember because it changes step-down planning.
LZD.shines: Useful for MRSA pneumonia logic and for VRE discussions when oral therapy matters.
LZD.trap: Myelosuppression, serotonin interactions, and prolonged-use toxicity are the exam traps.

DOX.summary: Flexible oral-heavy drug for atypicals, some skin infections, and selected MDR organisms like Stenotrophomonas.
DOX.shines: Easy teaching bridge between atypicals and outpatient-friendly therapy.
DOX.trap: It is not a universal staph or Gram-negative answer just because it comes in a tablet.

OMA.summary: Useful trainee card because it spans MRSA and atypicals while offering oral or IV flexibility.
OMA.shines: A clean example of a newer drug that changes oral step-down thinking without being universally first-line.
OMA.trap: It should stay a targeted tool, not a substitute for understanding the underlying syndrome.

GEN.summary: Aminoglycoside teaching value is often about synergy and careful use rather than mindless double coverage.
GEN.shines: Classic pair with ampicillin for enterococcal endocarditis teaching.
GEN.trap: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity quickly cancel any theoretical benefit when used badly.

MXF.summary: Worth a return mention because it still shows up where preserved susceptibility, atypical coverage, and some anaerobic reach are useful.
MXF.shines: A useful contrast drug: stronger respiratory and atypical framing than ciprofloxacin, but not an anti-pseudomonal answer.
MXF.trap: QT issues, collateral damage, and over-crediting its spectrum are the common mistakes.

SXT.summary: Commonly useful oral drug that trainees should remember for selected UTIs, skin infections, and Stenotrophomonas.
SXT.shines: A good teaching card for why oral options still matter in 2026 discussions.
SXT.trap: Potassium, creatinine interpretation, and resistance variation are the usual catches.

FOS.tagline: Older agent with selective MDR return
FOS.summary: A real return agent, but mostly in syndrome-specific and susceptibility-driven situations, especially urinary isolates and selected MDR combination strategies.
FOS.shines: Best remembered for resistant urinary Enterobacterales and as a mechanism-distinct partner rather than a universal salvage monotherapy.
FOS.trap: Its role is much narrower than a giant spectrum chart implies. Route, source, and regional IV access all matter.

CHL.summary: Historically broad, now mostly a niche or resource-limited salvage discussion because toxicity changed the risk-benefit balance.
CHL.shines: Useful on a trainee page because it reminds people that old broad agents sometimes reappear when options collapse.
CHL.trap: Do not romanticize it. Hematologic toxicity and limited modern routine use are the point.

MTZ.summary: The clearest anaerobe memory anchor on the page.
MTZ.shines: Important when a trainee needs to fix a regimen that forgot anaerobes.
MTZ.trap: It is not a broad abdominal drug on its own. It usually needs a partner.

AZM.summary: Still one of the easiest ways to remember atypical coverage.
AZM.shines: Useful when comparing macrolides against fluoroquinolones or doxycycline in atypical pneumonia thinking.
AZM.trap: It does not rescue beta-lactam failures against resistant typical pathogens.
